segments.text: Culture is the learned and shared way of life of a group. It includes ideas, values, beliefs, norms, language, customs and material objects. Culture tells people what things mean and what behaviour is considered appropriate in particular settings.
This is one of the largest and most important sociology topics. The easiest method is to divide it into characteristics, types, elements, socialization and cultural-contact concepts.

items.text: Characteristics of culture
: Culture is learned rather than biologically inherited, shared through groups, transmitted across generations, social, dynamic and adaptive. It varies across places and historical periods.
Material and non-material culture
: Material culture includes physical objects and technologies. Non-material culture includes beliefs, values, norms, symbols and language. The two influence each other.
Functions
: Culture transfers knowledge, defines situations, provides behaviour patterns, supports identity and shapes personality. It also gives people shared meanings that make coordination possible.
Elements

: norms, values, beliefs, sanctions, customs: Values are broad ideals; beliefs are ideas accepted as true; norms are expected rules of behaviour; sanctions are rewards or penalties encouraging conformity; customs are established practices.
Culture and socialization

: Socialization is the process by which people learn culture. Formal socialization occurs through organized instruction, while informal socialization occurs through ordinary interaction, observation and participation.
Cultural relativism

: Cultural relativism tries to understand a practice within its own cultural context before judging it. It is a method of understanding; it does not require ignoring universal legal or ethical concerns.
Subculture
: A subculture is a group within a wider society that shares distinctive values, styles or practices while still participating in the broader culture.
Ethnocentrism and xenocentrism
: Ethnocentrism judges other cultures through one’s own cultural standards and may assume one’s culture is superior. Xenocentrism idealizes another culture and may undervalue one’s own.
Cultural lag
: Cultural lag describes a situation where different parts of culture change at different speeds, for example when technology changes faster than laws or norms.
High and popular culture
: High culture usually refers to cultural forms historically associated with elite institutions; popular culture refers to widely consumed cultural forms. The boundary can change over time.
Multiculturalism, assimilation and acculturation

: Multiculturalism concerns coexistence and recognition of cultural diversity. Assimilation involves increasing absorption into another cultural pattern. Acculturation refers more broadly to cultural change through continuous contact between groups.

blocks.text: Culture as a learned system of meaning

segments.text: In sociology, culture means the learned and shared patterns through which people interpret the world and organize social life. It includes language, symbols, beliefs, values, norms, knowledge, technologies and ordinary practices. Culture is transmitted across generations but continuously modified through innovation, contact and conflict.

items.text: Learned
: Cultural behaviour is acquired through socialization rather than inherited as a complete biological program.
Shared
: Culture provides common meanings, but no society is perfectly homogeneous. Class, generation, region, ethnicity, occupation and other positions produce subcultural variation.
Symbolic
: Human beings use words, signs and objects to represent meanings beyond their physical form. Flags, uniforms, titles and rituals can organize loyalty and authority because of shared interpretation.
Dynamic
: Culture changes as new technologies, ideas, institutions and contacts alter practices. Continuity and change occur together.
Material culture
: Physical objects and technologies created or used by a society, such as buildings, tools, vehicles, clothing and communication devices.
Non-material culture
: Values, beliefs, language, norms, ideas and meanings. Material technologies often change behaviour only through non-material rules and expectations about how they should be used.
Interaction
: A smartphone is material culture; privacy norms, communication etiquette and ideas of availability are non-material culture. Social consequences arise from their interaction.

blocks.text: Core elements: values, beliefs, norms and sanctions

items.text: Values
: Broad ideals about what is desirable or important, such as justice, family responsibility, achievement or religious commitment. Values can conflict with one another in real decisions.
Beliefs
: Propositions people accept as true about the world. Beliefs may be religious, scientific, moral or everyday and are evaluated differently depending on the domain.
Norms
: Rules and expectations guiding behaviour. Folkways govern ordinary conventions, while mores concern stronger moral expectations; laws are formal norms enforced through state institutions.
Sanctions
: Rewards and penalties that reinforce norms. Informal sanctions include praise or ridicule; formal sanctions include grades, fines, dismissal or legal punishment.
Language
: Language stores and communicates cultural categories. It enables complex coordination while also reflecting social distinctions and power relations.
Ethnocentrism

: Judging another culture primarily by the standards of one's own can make unfamiliar practices appear irrational or inferior. Some degree of in-group preference is common, but strong ethnocentrism can support prejudice.
Cultural relativism

: A methodological principle of understanding a practice within its own cultural context before judging it. It does not require moral acceptance of every practice; sociologists can understand context while still analyzing harm, rights and power.
Analytical balance

: The goal is neither uncritical condemnation nor uncritical acceptance. Good sociology asks what a practice means locally, how it developed, who benefits, who is harmed and how insiders themselves debate it.
Subculture
: A group with distinctive norms, styles or practices within a wider society. Subcultures share many features with the wider culture while maintaining particular identities.
Counterculture
: A group that deliberately rejects important dominant values or practices and promotes alternatives.
Assimilation
: A process through which a group increasingly adopts the cultural patterns of another or of the wider society. It may be voluntary, pressured or uneven across domains.
Acculturation
: Broader change resulting from sustained contact between cultural groups. Both groups can change, and individuals may combine practices rather than replacing one identity completely.
Multiculturalism
: Institutional recognition of cultural diversity while members share a common political framework. Debates concern equality, integration, group rights and social cohesion.

segments.text: William F. Ogburn used cultural lag to describe cases in which material or technological change occurs faster than related norms, laws or institutions. Digital privacy is an easy example: new data technologies may spread before rules and public expectations adapt. Cultural lag is useful when it identifies a specific mismatch; it should not be used as a vague label for every disagreement about modernity.

rows: Avoid this error Do not confuse “culture” with only art, food and dress. In sociology it includes the full system of learned meanings, norms, values and practices.

blocks.text: How to Build an Examination Answer

segments.text: Define culture, explain characteristics, types and functions, then elements, socialization and cultural-contact concepts. Use short examples to make distinctions clear.
• Conerly, Holmes, & Tamang, Introduction to Sociology 3e (OpenStax, 2021).
• William F. Ogburn, Social Change with Respect to Culture and Original Nature (1922), for cultural-lag concept.
• Culture is learned, shared and transmitted.
• Norms are rules; values are ideals; sanctions enforce norms.
• Cultural relativism helps avoid judging every society solely by one’s own standards.
• Connect definitions with mechanisms, examples and limitations; do not present the topic as a list of isolated terms.
